answer: Amber's Z-value peaked in the 4th millennium BCE, with a maximum of 1.54 sustained over the 3300–3000 BCE interval (Middle Neolithic, "MN"). This is the global maximum and is distinct from a secondary, lower plateau of 1.46 at 4000–3400 BCE that lies just before it (not the peak). Because the data are binned at 100-year resolution, the interval is stated at bin level — the four bins 3300, 3200, 3100, and 3000 BCE all equal 1.54 — not to a single year. The 3000 BCE bin sits on the 4th/3rd-millennium boundary, so the peak is attributed to the 4th millennium BCE.

payload.workflow: Loaded data/time_series_data.csv (BCE = -CE, verified vs calBP) and data/capital.csv (comma decimals). Computed the global maximum of the amber Z-value and the extent of the plateau where Z equals that max, using time_series_data.csv Amber_inter (interpolated, 3601 rows) cross-checked against raw Amber (37 values at 100-yr bins) and capital.csv Zamber (100-yr bins). All three agree: max Z = 1.54 over 3300-3000 BCE (group MN). Assigned the millennium via standard BCE convention (4th millennium = 4000-3001 BCE). Also identified the secondary 1.46 plateau at 4000-3400 BCE to confirm it is not the peak.
